questions.sub: Motor Hierarchy: Motor Cortex, Premotor/SMA, Brainstem, and Spinal Cord
questions.q: Which cerebral cortical area contains Betz giant pyramidal neurons and serves as the primary origin of corticospinal fibers controlling discrete, fractionated movements of distal contralateral limb muscles (especially hand/finger digits)?
options: Primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4 in the precentral gyrus)
Primary somatosensory cortex (Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2 in the postcentral gyrus)
Superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 22)
Calcarine sulcus (Brodmann area 17)
questions.explain: Brodmann area 4 in the precentral gyrus houses Betz cells and projects directly onto spinal motor neurons/interneurons for fine contralateral distal control; supplementary motor area (SMA, area 6) and premotor cortex plan and sequence movements.

open.q: Which cortical region contains Betz giant pyramidal cells and primarily governs fine, fractionated voluntary movements of contralateral distal limb muscles?
accept: Primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4)
Primary motor cortex
Precentral gyrus (Brodmann area 4)

questions.sub: Motor Hierarchy: Motor Cortex, Premotor/SMA, Brainstem, and Spinal Cord
questions.q: How do the 'supplementary motor area (SMA)' and 'premotor cortex' (both in Brodmann area 6) contribute differently to movement planning and execution?
options: SMA supports self-initiated sequences and bimanual movement; premotor cortex selects externally cued movements and prepares posture
SMA controls eye muscles; premotor cortex processes taste
Both areas lie in the occipital lobe and process colour vision
Premotor cortex fires only after spinal motor neurons stop firing
questions.explain: SMA drives self-initiated sequences and bimanual coordination (and activates even during imagined movement), whereas lateral premotor cortex links external visual/sensory cues to motor selection and proximal trunk/girdle stabilization.

open.q: Contrast the primary functional roles of the supplementary motor area (SMA) and the premotor cortex in motor planning.
accept: SMA coordinates internally generated, sequential, and bimanual movements (and motor imagery), whereas premotor cortex guides externally/visually cued movements and proximal posture/girdle preparation
SMA: internally generated/sequential/bimanual movements; Premotor cortex: externally cued movements and proximal stabilization

questions.sub: Descending Tracts: Lateral vs Ventromedial Pathways
questions.q: Contrast the 'lateral corticospinal tract (pyramidal tract)' with the 'ventromedial brainstem pathways' (vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, and tectospinal tracts) in anatomical termination and motor control:
options: Lateral corticospinal pathways control skilled distal movement; ventromedial brainstem pathways regulate posture, balance and axial/proximal muscles
Ventromedial pathways control fine finger movements; lateral corticospinal pathways control only axial posture
Both systems remain uncrossed and terminate exclusively in the cerebellum
Vestibulospinal pathways supply only intrinsic hand muscles
questions.explain: Lateral descending systems (lateral corticospinal and rubrospinal tracts) govern contralateral distal limb movement and fine motor skill; ventromedial systems (vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, tectospinal, anterior corticospinal) govern bilateral axial posture, balance, and orienting.

open.q: Compare the anatomical targets and movement functions of the lateral corticospinal tract versus the ventromedial descending motor pathways.
accept: Lateral corticospinal tract crosses at the medullary pyramids and targets contralateral distal limb motor neurons for fine, fractionated voluntary movement; ventromedial tracts target bilateral proximal/axial/girdle motor neurons to control posture, balance, and gross movement
Lateral corticospinal: contralateral distal fine movement; Ventromedial: bilateral proximal/axial posture and balance

questions.sub: Descending Tracts: Lateral vs Ventromedial Pathways
questions.q: Why does a lesion of the 'lateral corticospinal tract' impair fine individual finger movements ('fractionation') while leaving gross whole-hand grasp and proximal posture relatively preserved?
options: Lateral CST loss removes direct distal corticomotoneuronal control; brainstem tracts preserve gross posture and grasp
Fine finger movements are controlled by the olfactory nerve
The spinal cord generates fine finger movements without descending input
The lateral corticospinal tract only inhibits the diaphragm
questions.explain: Loss of direct corticomotoneuronal connections eliminates independent digit control (causing loss of fine finger dexterity and Babinski sign), while brainstem reticulospinal/vestibulospinal pathways maintain gross posture and synergistic movements. Key detail: Loss of direct corticomotoneuronal drive impairs independent finger control, while brainstem pathways preserve gross synergistic and proximal movements.

open.q: Explain why damage to the lateral corticospinal tract abolishes fine independent finger movements while sparing gross postural support and synergistic limb movements.
accept: Brainstem ventromedial pathways (reticulospinal and vestibulospinal tracts) and rubrospinal/uncrossed fibers still support posture and gross synergistic movements, whereas direct corticospinal input needed for independent distal digit control is lost
Intact reticulospinal/vestibulospinal and rubrospinal pathways maintain gross posture while direct corticospinal drive for isolated finger control is lost

questions.sub: Descending Tracts: Lateral vs Ventromedial Pathways
questions.q: How do the 'pontine reticulospinal tract' and 'medullary reticulospinal tract' exert opposing influences on spinal antigravity (extensor) motor neurons?
options: Pontine reticulospinal activity excites antigravity extensors; medullary reticulospinal activity inhibits extensors and favours flexors
Pontine reticulospinal tract inhibits all muscles while medullary reticulospinal tract excites only eye muscles
Both tracts originate in the primary visual cortex
Neither tract communicates with spinal motor neurons
questions.explain: Tonic excitatory drive from the pontine reticular formation promotes extensor tone unless balanced by cortical/cerebellar activation of the inhibitory medullary reticular formation.

open.q: Contrast the opposing effects of the pontine reticulospinal tract and medullary reticulospinal tract on spinal extensor motor neurons.
accept: Pontine reticulospinal tract excites spinal extensor (antigravity) motor neurons, whereas the medullary reticulospinal tract inhibits spinal extensor motor neurons
Pontine reticulospinal excites extensors; medullary reticulospinal inhibits extensors

questions.sub: Descending Tracts: Lateral vs Ventromedial Pathways
questions.q: Which descending tract originates in the 'superior colliculus' of the midbrain and mediates reflexive head and eye turning toward sudden visual, auditory, or somatosensory stimuli?
options: Tectospinal tract
Lateral corticospinal tract
Dorsal column-medial lemniscal tract
Spinothalamic tract
questions.explain: The tectospinal tract descends from the superior colliculus to upper cervical segments to orient the head and neck reflexively toward unexpected sensory stimuli.

open.q: Which descending tract arises from the superior colliculus to coordinate reflexive head and neck turning toward sudden sensory stimuli?
accept: Tectospinal tract
Tectospinal

questions.sub: Posture and Muscle Tone: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation, Stretch Reflex, and Decerebrate Rigidity
questions.q: What is 'alpha-gamma coactivation', and why must gamma motor neurons fire together with alpha motor neurons during voluntary muscle contraction?
options: Alpha motor neurons shorten extrafusal fibres while gamma motor neurons keep intrafusal spindle fibres taut and sensitive
Alpha motor neurons supply intrafusal fibres while gamma motor neurons supply extrafusal fibres
Gamma activity silences spindle afferents during voluntary movement
Alpha-gamma coactivation prevents skeletal muscle contraction
questions.explain: If gamma motor neurons did not co-activate when extrafusal fibers shorten, the muscle spindle would go slack and stop firing Ia afferents; coactivation keeps the spindle taut and responsive to unexpected load changes during active shortening.

open.q: Explain why alpha-gamma coactivation is required during voluntary muscle shortening to maintain muscle spindle function.
accept: Gamma motor neurons contract the polar ends of intrafusal muscle spindle fibers as extrafusal fibers shorten, preventing spindle slack and keeping Ia stretch afferents sensitive throughout active movement
Prevents muscle spindle slack during shortening so Ia afferents continue signaling length/stretch changes

questions.sub: Posture and Muscle Tone: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation, Stretch Reflex, and Decerebrate Rigidity
questions.q: Contrast 'gamma-dynamic' and 'gamma-static' motor neurons in regulating muscle spindle sensitivity:
options: Dynamic gamma: bag1/velocity sensitivity; static gamma: bag2 and chain/steady-length sensitivity
Dynamic gamma neurons inhibit all stretch reflexes while static gamma neurons cause paralysis
Static gamma neurons innervate only extrafusal fibres
Dynamic gamma neurons are located in the olfactory bulb
questions.explain: Dynamic gamma boosts velocity sensitivity via bag1 intrafusal fibers; static gamma sustains steady-state length sensitivity via bag2 and chain fibers and prevents Ia unloading during shortening. Key detail: Dynamic gamma neurons target bag1 fibres and increase velocity sensitivity; static gamma neurons target bag2 and chain fibres and support steady-length sensitivity.

open.q: Distinguish the functional effects of dynamic gamma versus static gamma motor neurons on muscle spindle afferents.
accept: Dynamic gamma motor neurons heighten Ia sensitivity to the velocity/rate of muscle stretch, whereas static gamma motor neurons sustain afferent firing to static muscle length and steady stretch
Dynamic gamma enhances rate/velocity sensitivity; static gamma maintains steady-state length sensitivity

questions.sub: Posture and Muscle Tone: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation, Stretch Reflex, and Decerebrate Rigidity
questions.q: What is 'decerebrate rigidity' (extensor posturing), which anatomical transection classically produces it in experimental physiology, and why does it occur?
options: Intercollicular transection leaves vestibulospinal and pontine reticulospinal extensor drive relatively unopposed
Transection below the lumbar enlargement removes all extensor tone
Destruction of vestibular nuclei produces severe extensor rigidity
An isolated peripheral nerve lesion produces bilateral extensor posturing
questions.explain: Intercollicular decerebration leaves the pontine reticular formation and lateral vestibular nucleus intact while disconnecting higher inhibitory/modulatory inputs (cortex, red nucleus, medullary reticular formation), producing marked antigravity extensor rigidity.

open.q: State the brainstem transection level that produces classic decerebrate rigidity and explain the balance of excitatory versus inhibitory pathways driving the extensor rigidity.
accept: Midbrain (intercollicular level, between superior and inferior colliculi); unopposed excitatory drive from the lateral vestibular nucleus and pontine reticular formation predominates after losing higher cortical/rubral/medullary inhibitory modulation
Midbrain intercollicular transection; unopposed pontine reticulospinal and lateral vestibulospinal excitation of extensors

questions.sub: Posture and Muscle Tone: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation, Stretch Reflex, and Decerebrate Rigidity
questions.q: What is 'decorticate posturing' (decorticate rigidity), and how does it differ anatomically from decerebrate posturing?
options: Flexed upper limbs and extended lower limbs after a lesion above the midbrain, with rubrospinal flexor influence preserved
Complete flaccidity of all four limbs with absent tendon reflexes
Upper-limb extension and lower-limb flexion caused by cerebellar tumour alone
Involuntary rhythmic blinking without limb posturing
questions.explain: In decorticate posturing, the red nucleus and rubrospinal tract remain intact above the brainstem lesion, promoting upper-limb flexor tone while lower limbs extend under vestibulospinal/reticulospinal influence.

open.q: Describe the limb posture in decorticate posturing and explain why the upper limbs flex while the lower limbs extend.
accept: Upper limbs flexed (elbows/wrists flexed, arms adducted) and lower limbs extended; occurs with lesions above the midbrain where an intact red nucleus/rubrospinal tract promotes upper-limb flexion while brainstem extensor tracts drive lower-limb extension
Upper-limb flexion and lower-limb extension; spared rubrospinal tract favors upper-limb flexors while brainstem tracts drive leg extension

questions.sub: Cerebellum: Functional Divisions, Circuitry, and Motor Learning
questions.q: Match the three functional divisions of the cerebellum with their primary inputs, outputs, and motor functions:
options: Vestibulocerebellum: balance/VOR; spinocerebellum: posture/gait; cerebrocerebellum: planning/timing
Vestibulocerebellum: speech; spinocerebellum: hearing; cerebrocerebellum: pupillary reflexes
Vestibulocerebellum: fine finger movement; spinocerebellum: smell; cerebrocerebellum: balance only
All three divisions have identical inputs and functions
questions.explain: Memorize the deep nuclei rule ('Don't Eat Greasy Food, Ever' from lateral to medial: Dentate -> Emboliform -> Globose -> Fastigial) and map each division to its core function: balance/eye movements, posture/gait & limb execution, and motor planning/timing. Key detail: Vestibulocerebellum: balance and eye movements; spinocerebellum: posture, gait and limb execution; cerebrocerebellum: planning and timing skilled movement.

open.q: Match the vestibulocerebellum, spinocerebellum (vermis and paravermis), and cerebrocerebellum with their primary motor roles and deep cerebellar nuclei.
accept: Vestibulocerebellum: balance, equilibrium, and eye movements (vestibular nuclei); Spinocerebellum: axial posture/gait via vermis (fastigial nucleus) and limb movement execution via paravermis (interpositus/globose-emboliform nuclei); Cerebrocerebellum: motor planning, timing, and skilled coordination (dentate nucleus)
Vestibulocerebellum (balance/eye movements); Spinocerebellum (posture/gait via fastigial; limb execution via interpositus); Cerebrocerebellum (motor planning/timing via dentate)

questions.sub: Cerebellum: Functional Divisions, Circuitry, and Motor Learning
questions.q: In the cerebellar cortex, which cell type is the SOLE output neuron projecting to the deep cerebellar nuclei, and is its neurotransmitter excitatory or inhibitory?
options: Purkinje cell — GABAergic (INHIBITORY) output onto deep cerebellar and vestibular nuclei
Granule cell — GABAergic inhibitory output
Mossy fiber — cholinergic excitatory output from Purkinje cells
Climbing fiber — dopaminergic output from Purkinje cells
questions.explain: Purkinje cells provide the sole inhibitory (GABA) output of the cerebellar cortex onto the deep cerebellar nuclei; mossy fibers (via granule cell parallel fibers) and climbing fibers (from the inferior olivary nucleus) are EXCITATORY inputs.

open.q: Which cerebellar cortical neuron forms the sole output from the cerebellar cortex, and what neurotransmitter does it release?
accept: Purkinje cell; releases GABA (inhibitory)
Purkinje cell; GABA (inhibitory neurotransmitter)

questions.sub: Cerebellum: Functional Divisions, Circuitry, and Motor Learning
questions.q: How do 'climbing fibers' originating from the 'inferior olivary nucleus' contribute to cerebellar motor learning ('error correction')?
options: Climbing fibres signal motor error; their co-activation with parallel fibres can induce LTD at parallel-fibre–Purkinje synapses
Climbing fibres myelinate Purkinje dendrites to increase firing rate
Climbing fibres permanently inhibit the inferior olive after one movement
Climbing fibres release acetylcholine onto skeletal muscle endplates
questions.explain: Climbing-fiber error signals trigger Ca2+ influx in Purkinje dendrites that depresses ('LTD') mismatched parallel-fiber synapses, calibrating motor accuracy across trials.

open.q: Explain the role of climbing fibers from the inferior olive and long-term depression (LTD) at Purkinje cell synapses in cerebellar motor learning.
accept: Climbing fibers signal motor errors/unexpected sensory events to Purkinje cells, inducing long-term depression (LTD) at concurrently active parallel-fiber synapses to calibrate and refine movement accuracy
Signal motor errors to Purkinje cells and induce LTD at parallel-fiber synapses to correct movement errors

questions.sub: Cerebellum: Functional Divisions, Circuitry, and Motor Learning
questions.q: Why does a unilateral cerebellar lesion produce 'IPSILATERAL' motor signs (ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia) despite cerebellar output ascending to the contralateral motor cortex?
options: Cerebellar output crosses to the opposite cortex; corticospinal fibres cross back at the pyramids, causing ipsilateral signs
Cerebellar output never crosses, but corticospinal output crosses twice in the spinal cord
Cerebellar lesions cause contralateral signs because both pathways remain uncrossed
Only sensory pathways cross, so cerebellar signs are always bilateral
questions.explain: Double crossing—first via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the opposite thalamus/cortex, then via the pyramidal decussation back to the original side—means unilateral cerebellar damage produces ipsilateral limb signs. Key detail: Double crossing—cerebellar output to the opposite cortex, then corticospinal fibres back across at the pyramidal decussation—produces ipsilateral signs.

open.q: Explain the neuroanatomical 'double decussation' that causes a unilateral cerebellar lesion to produce ipsilateral motor signs.
accept: Cerebellar output crosses to the contralateral thalamus/motor cortex, and the descending corticospinal tract crosses back to the ipsilateral side in the medullary pyramids, resulting in ipsilateral symptoms
Output crosses to the opposite thalamus/cortex and corticospinal fibers cross back in the pyramids, producing ipsilateral signs

questions.sub: Cerebellum: Functional Divisions, Circuitry, and Motor Learning
questions.q: Match these classic cerebellar clinical signs with their definitions: 'dysmetria', 'intention tremor', and 'dysdiadochokinesia':
options: Dysmetria: range error; intention tremor: target approach; dysdiadochokinesia: rapid alternation
Intention tremor occurs only at rest while dysmetria means muscle weakness
Dysdiadochokinesia means complete loss of vision in both eyes
Dysmetria is involuntary chorea of the tongue
questions.explain: Cerebellar tremor is a kinetic/intention tremor appearing during targeted movement (unlike Parkinsonian resting 'pill-rolling' tremor), paired with dysmetria (past-pointing) and dysdiadochokinesia. Key detail: Dysmetria: inaccurate movement range; intention tremor: tremor during target-directed movement; dysdiadochokinesia: impaired rapid alternating movements.

open.q: Define dysmetria, intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia as manifestations of cerebellar dysfunction.
accept: Dysmetria: impaired judgment of movement distance/range (past-pointing); Intention tremor: tremor worsening during purposeful target approach; Dysdiadochokinesia: impaired rapid alternating movements
Dysmetria: impaired range/past-pointing; Intention tremor: tremor worsening near target; Dysdiadochokinesia: impaired rapid alternating movements

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia: Direct, Indirect, and Nigrostriatal Pathways
questions.q: Which neurotransmitter does the 'striatum (caudate and putamen)' receive from the 'substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc)' via the 'nigrostriatal pathway', and what are its differential effects on D1 versus D2 medium spiny neurons?
options: Dopamine excites D1 direct-pathway neurons and inhibits D2 indirect-pathway neurons, favouring movement
Acetylcholine inhibits all striatal neurons equally
GABA excites SNc neurons to stop all movement
Glutamate permanently blocks dopamine synthesis
questions.explain: Dopamine acting on D1 (excitatory) and D2 (inhibitory) receptors in the striatum shifts the net balance toward movement initiation by disinhibiting thalamocortical motor neurons.

open.q: Name the neurotransmitter of the nigrostriatal pathway and explain its opposing actions on D1 versus D2 striatal neurons.
accept: Dopamine; excites D1 receptors on the direct (movement-facilitating) pathway and inhibits D2 receptors on the indirect (movement-inhibiting) pathway
Dopamine; excites D1 (direct pathway) and inhibits D2 (indirect pathway)

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia: Direct, Indirect, and Nigrostriatal Pathways
questions.q: Trace how activation of the 'direct pathway' in the basal ganglia facilitates voluntary movement ('disinhibition'):
options: Striatal inhibition of GPi/SNr reduces their inhibition of the motor thalamus, disinhibiting thalamocortical output
Striatum excites GPi to strongly inhibit the thalamus
Motor thalamus directly inhibits primary motor cortex
GPi releases dopamine onto skeletal muscle fibres
questions.explain: GPi/SNr neurons fire tonically to hold the motor thalamus under inhibitory brake; the direct pathway inhibits GPi/SNr ('inhibition of an inhibition' = disinhibition), releasing the thalamus to excite motor cortex.

open.q: Trace the synaptic connections of the basal ganglia direct pathway and explain why it is called a 'disinhibitory' circuit.
accept: Striatum inhibits GPi/SNr, which reduces tonic GABAergic inhibition of the motor thalamus (VA/VL), thereby disinhibiting/exciting thalamocortical projections to motor cortex
Striatum inhibits GPi/SNr -> reduces tonic inhibition on motor thalamus -> increases thalamocortical excitation of motor cortex

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia: Direct, Indirect, and Nigrostriatal Pathways
questions.q: Trace how the 'indirect pathway' (striatum -> external globus pallidus -> subthalamic nucleus -> GPi/SNr -> thalamus) suppresses unwanted movements:
options: Striatum inhibits GPe, disinhibiting STN; STN excites GPi/SNr, increasing inhibition of the motor thalamus
Striatum excites GPe to inhibit STN and increase thalamic excitation
Subthalamic nucleus releases GABA to inhibit GPi
Indirect pathway bypasses GPi/SNr completely
questions.explain: Whereas the direct pathway disinhibits the thalamus to promote movement, the indirect pathway boosts subthalamic glutamatergic drive onto GPi/SNr to increase thalamic inhibition and suppress competing/unwanted movements.

open.q: Trace the indirect pathway through the external globus pallidus (GPe) and subthalamic nucleus (STN) and explain its net effect on the motor thalamus.
accept: Striatum inhibits GPe -> disinhibits excitatory subthalamic nucleus (STN) -> STN excites GPi/SNr -> increases GABAergic inhibition of the motor thalamus (decreasing thalamocortical drive)
Striatum inhibits GPe -> disinhibits STN -> excites GPi/SNr -> increases inhibition of motor thalamus

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia: Direct, Indirect, and Nigrostriatal Pathways
questions.q: Which neurotransmitter does the 'subthalamic nucleus (STN)' use to excite the internal and external globus pallidus (GPi and GPe)?
options: Glutamate (excitatory)
GABA (inhibitory)
Dopamine
Glycine
questions.explain: Within the basal ganglia, the subthalamic nucleus (STN) is the major excitatory glutamatergic nucleus, whereas the striatum, GPe, GPi, and SNr are predominantly GABAergic.

open.q: Which excitatory neurotransmitter is released by neurons of the subthalamic nucleus (STN)?
accept: Glutamate
L-glutamate

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia: Direct, Indirect, and Nigrostriatal Pathways
questions.q: Contrast 'hypokinetic movement disorders' (such as Parkinson's disease) with 'hyperkinetic movement disorders' (such as Huntington's disease or hemiballismus) in terms of basal ganglia output onto the motor thalamus:
options: Hypokinetic disorders increase GPi/SNr inhibition of the motor thalamus; hyperkinetic disorders reduce it
Hyperkinetic disorders cause excessive thalamic inhibition while hypokinetic disorders cause ballismus
Basal ganglia output to the thalamus is identical in Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases
Hypokinetic disorders are caused by excess striatal dopamine
questions.explain: In Parkinson's disease, loss of nigrostriatal dopamine shifts balance toward excessive GPi/SNr inhibition of the thalamus (hypokinesia); in Huntington's disease, early loss of indirect-pathway striatal neurons reduces GPi inhibition of the thalamus, causing choreiform hyperkinesia.

open.q: Contrast GPi/SNr inhibitory output onto the motor thalamus in hypokinetic versus hyperkinetic basal ganglia disorders.
accept: Hypokinetic disorders show increased GPi/SNr inhibition of the motor thalamus (causing bradykinesia/rigidity), whereas hyperkinetic disorders show decreased GPi/SNr inhibition of the motor thalamus (causing involuntary movements like chorea or ballismus)
Increased GPi/SNr inhibition of thalamus (hypokinetic) vs decreased GPi/SNr inhibition of thalamus (hyperkinetic)

questions.sub: Locomotion and Spinal Circuits: Central Pattern Generators, Reciprocal Innervation, and Gait
questions.q: What are 'spinal central pattern generators (CPGs)', and how do they generate rhythmic walking/stepping movements even without supraspinal commands or rhythmic sensory feedback?
options: Spinal interneuron networks generate alternating flexor-extensor rhythms, modulated by descending commands and sensory feedback
Pacemaker cells inside the primary visual cortex
Direct skeletal muscle contraction without motor neurons
Reflexes requiring the olfactory bulb for every step
questions.explain: Decerebrate or spinalized animals with appropriate sensory/pharmacological support can still generate coordinated stepping rhythms because spinal CPG interneuron circuits generate the core alternating flexor-extensor pattern.

open.q: Define spinal central pattern generators (CPGs) and state their role in rhythmic locomotion.
accept: Intrinsic spinal cord interneuron networks that generate rhythmic, alternating flexor and extensor motor patterns for locomotion/stepping without requiring rhythmic sensory input or continuous cortical commands
Intrinsic spinal interneuron circuits generating rhythmic alternating flexor-extensor bursts for locomotion

questions.sub: Locomotion and Spinal Circuits: Central Pattern Generators, Reciprocal Innervation, and Gait
questions.q: How does 'reciprocal innervation' work during a monosynaptic stretch reflex or a flexor withdrawal reflex?
options: Ia afferents excite agonist motor neurons and activate inhibitory interneurons that suppress antagonist motor neurons
Motor neurons excite agonist and antagonist muscles equally
Sensory afferents inhibit all spinal motor neurons
Reciprocal innervation occurs only in gastric smooth muscle
questions.explain: During knee extension or flexor withdrawal, inhibitory Ia/spinal interneurons relax opposing antagonist muscles so limb motion is smooth and unopposed.

open.q: Explain the neural mechanism of reciprocal innervation between agonist and antagonist muscles in the spinal cord.
accept: Excitation of agonist alpha motor neurons is paired with activation of inhibitory interneurons (such as Ia inhibitory interneurons) that hyperpolarize antagonist alpha motor neurons, relaxing opposing muscles
Agonist motor neurons are excited while antagonist motor neurons are inhibited via inhibitory interneurons

questions.sub: Locomotion and Spinal Circuits: Central Pattern Generators, Reciprocal Innervation, and Gait
questions.q: What is 'recurrent (Renshaw cell) inhibition' in the ventral horn of the spinal cord?
options: Alpha-motor axon collaterals excite Renshaw cells, which inhibit the same motor pool and related interneurons
Sympathetic fibres excite sensory dorsal root ganglion cells
Botulinum toxin facilitates acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Cerebellar Purkinje cells directly excite skeletal muscle
questions.explain: Renshaw cells form a classic negative-feedback recurrent loop onto alpha motor neurons, dampening excessive firing and helping focus motor output.

open.q: Describe the recurrent circuit involving alpha motor neuron axon collaterals and Renshaw cells, and state its functional effect.
accept: Alpha motor neuron axon collaterals excite Renshaw interneurons, which project back to inhibit the alpha motor neuron (and Ia inhibitory interneurons), providing negative feedback to stabilize firing and sharpen motor output
Motor neuron collaterals excite Renshaw cells which feed back to inhibit the motor neuron (negative feedback)

questions.sub: Locomotion and Spinal Circuits: Central Pattern Generators, Reciprocal Innervation, and Gait
questions.q: Compare the two major phases of the human walking gait cycle ('stance phase' versus 'swing phase') and their approximate share of the cycle:
options: Stance occupies about 60% of the gait cycle; swing occupies about 40%
Swing accounts for 85% of walking and stance 15%
Both feet are off the ground throughout stance
Slow walking has no stance phase
questions.explain: During normal walking, stance occupies ~60% of the stride (with double-limb support at beginning and end of stance) and swing occupies ~40%; as speed increases to running, double support disappears and periods of aerial float appear.

open.q: State the approximate percentage of the walking gait cycle spent in the stance phase versus the swing phase and describe what the foot is doing in each.
accept: Stance phase (~60%): foot contacts the ground and bears weight/propels the body; Swing phase (~40%): foot clears the ground and swings forward
Stance (~60%, foot on ground bearing weight) and swing (~40%, foot off ground advancing forward)

questions.sub: Locomotion and Spinal Circuits: Central Pattern Generators, Reciprocal Innervation, and Gait
questions.q: Which muscle group contracts to 'dorsiflex' the ankle during the 'swing phase' of gait so the toes clear the ground without dragging ('foot drop')?
options: Deep peroneal-innervated anterior compartment dorsiflexors (tibialis anterior, EHL and EDL)
Gastrocnemius and soleus (tibial nerve)
Gluteus maximus (inferior gluteal nerve)
Iliopsoas (femoral nerve)
questions.explain: Weakness of tibialis anterior / deep peroneal nerve (e.g., common fibular nerve palsy at the fibular neck or L5 radiculopathy) causes 'foot drop' and a compensatory 'steppage gait' (high knee lift) to keep toes from scraping the floor during swing. Key detail: Anterior compartment ankle dorsiflexors (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus), innervated by the deep peroneal (fibular) nerve (L4-L5).

open.q: Which muscle and nerve produce ankle dorsiflexion during the swing phase of walking to prevent toe-dragging (foot drop)?
accept: Tibialis anterior (and anterior compartment dorsiflexors) innervated by the deep peroneal (fibular) nerve
Tibialis anterior; deep peroneal (fibular) nerve

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 62-year-old man with hypertension presents 4 hours after sudden onset of right-sided weakness. Exam reveals spastic paralysis of the right arm and leg, hyperreflexia, sustained ankle clonus, loss of superficial abdominal reflexes on the right, and an upgoing right big toe (dorsiflexion with fanning of toes) on plantar stroking ('Babinski sign'). Where is the primary lesion located?
options: Left upper motor neuron (UMN) pathway—such as the left internal capsule (posterior limb) or left primary motor cortex/corticospinal tract
Right peripheral sciatic nerve (lower motor neuron)
Right neuromuscular junction
Left cerebellar flocculus
questions.explain: Spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and a positive Babinski sign (extensor plantar response) are hallmark signs of an upper motor neuron (corticospinal) lesion contralateral to the deficit.

open.q: Which class of motor neuron lesion (upper vs lower) and which side of the CNS is indicated by contralateral spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and a positive Babinski sign?
accept: Contralateral upper motor neuron (UMN / corticospinal tract) lesion
Upper motor neuron lesion on the opposite side

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 49-year-old man has a fracture of the fibular neck on his right leg and walks into clinic lifting his right knee high with each step to keep his right toes from dragging on the ground ('steppage gait'), with inability to dorsiflex or evert the right foot and decreased sensation over the dorsal foot and first web space. Which nerve is injured and what type of motor deficit is present?
options: Right common fibular nerve palsy causing LMN foot drop with weak dorsiflexion and eversion
Left lateral corticospinal tract—an upper motor neuron lesion with spasticity and clonus
Right femoral nerve—spastic knee extension
Right obturator nerve—adductor spasticity
questions.explain: Peripheral nerve injury at the fibular neck damages lower motor neurons (common/deep/superficial peroneal fibers), producing flaccid foot drop, steppage gait, and reduced/absent local reflexes rather than spasticity. Key detail: Right common peroneal (fibular) nerve—a LOWER motor neuron (LMN) lesion causing flaccid weakness/paralysis of dorsiflexion and eversion, muscle atrophy, hyporeflexia, and fasciculations/denervation.

open.q: Identify the injured nerve and motor neuron classification (UMN vs LMN) in a patient with right foot drop and steppage gait after a fibular neck fracture.
accept: Right common peroneal (fibular) nerve; lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion
Common fibular (peroneal) nerve; lower motor neuron lesion

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 67-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of progressive resting tremor ('pill-rolling' tremor of the thumb and index finger that diminishes during voluntary reaching), cogwheel/lead-pipe muscle rigidity, slowness of movement (bradykinesia), masked facial expression (hypomimia), and a shuffling gait with reduced arm swing. Which pathological loss causes these signs?
options: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta
Loss of GABAergic neurons in the striatum
Loss of Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex
Loss of lower motor neurons in the anterior horn
questions.explain: Parkinson's disease is driven by loss of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the SNc (with Lewy bodies containing alpha-synuclein), reducing direct-pathway facilitation and increasing indirect-pathway brake activity.

open.q: Which midbrain nucleus degenerates in Parkinson's disease to cause bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor, and which neurotransmitter is depleted in the striatum?
accept: Substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc); depletes dopamine in the striatum
Substantia nigra pars compacta; dopamine

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 42-year-old man whose father died of a progressive neurodegenerative movement disorder develops involuntary, brief, irregular, dancelike movements of his face, trunk, and limbs (chorea), irritability, and cognitive decline. Genetic testing shows CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4. Which striatal neurons are lost earliest in this disorder?
options: GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the striatum (especially those projecting to the external globus pallidus in the INDIRECT pathway)
Motor neurons of the abducens nucleus
Hair cells of the cochlear apex
Anterior horn cells of the cervical cord
questions.explain: Huntington's disease (autosomal dominant HTT CAG expansion) causes early degeneration of striatal GABAergic neurons—particularly indirect-pathway neurons—releasing the motor thalamus from inhibition and producing chorea.

open.q: Which striatal neuronal population degenerates early in Huntington's disease to disinhibit the motor thalamus and produce chorea?
accept: GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the striatum (particularly indirect-pathway neurons projecting to the external globus pallidus)
Striatal GABAergic medium spiny neurons (especially indirect pathway)

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 69-year-old woman with sudden-onset lacunar stroke in the deep brain develops violent, wide-amplitude, flinging/hurling movements of her left arm and leg ('hemiballismus') that occur unpredictably even at rest. Which small contralateral structure is infarcted?
options: Right subthalamic nucleus (STN)
Left medial geniculate nucleus
Right vestibular nuclei
Left olfactory tract
questions.explain: A lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus (STN) removes excitatory glutamatergic drive onto GPi/SNr, markedly reducing GPi inhibition of the motor thalamus and releasing wild, flinging contralateral limb movements (hemiballismus).

open.q: Which contralateral structure is damaged to produce sudden, violent flinging movements of the limbs (hemiballismus)?
accept: Contralateral subthalamic nucleus (STN)
Subthalamic nucleus

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 58-year-old man with chronic alcohol use disorder presents with a wide-based, staggering ('drunken') gait, truncal sway when standing or sitting even with eyes open, and slurred scanning speech, while fine finger-to-nose testing in his arms is nearly normal. Which cerebellar region is predominantly atrophied?
options: Cerebellar vermis and flocculonodular lobe (midline/vestibulocerebellar degeneration classic in chronic alcoholism)
Left primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus)
Right caudate head
Left occipital pole
questions.explain: Chronic alcoholism (and thiamine/B1 deficiency) preferentially damages the anterior superior vermis and flocculonodular regions, causing prominent truncal and gait ataxia.

open.q: Which cerebellar region is classically affected in chronic alcohol-related gait and truncal ataxia?
accept: Cerebellar vermis (and flocculonodular lobe)
Cerebellar vermis

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 38-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has a demyelinating plaque in the left cerebellar hemisphere / middle and superior cerebellar peduncles. On neurological exam, she exhibits left-sided past-pointing (dysmetria), left-sided intention tremor on finger-to-nose testing, and inability to perform rapid alternating hand taps on the left (dysdiadochokinesia). Why are her symptoms on the LEFT side?
options: Cerebellar pathways double-cross, so left cerebellar lesions cause ipsilateral limb signs
The left cerebellum controls the right arm directly without crossing
Multiple sclerosis affects only ipsilateral motor neurons in the left hand
Left cerebellar lesions cause right-sided blindness instead of ataxia
questions.explain: Unilateral cerebellar lesions cause ipsilateral motor coordination deficits (ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia) because of the double crossing between cerebellum, thalamus/cortex, and medullary pyramids. Key detail: Cerebellar motor pathways undergo a double decussation (cerebellothalamic crossing to right thalamus/cortex, then corticospinal crossing back to left spinal cord), so unilateral left cerebellar lesions cause ipsilateral left limb signs.

open.q: Why does a lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere produce ataxia and dysmetria in the left arm rather than the right arm?
accept: Cerebellar outflow crosses to the right thalamus/cortex and descending corticospinal fibers cross back to the left in the medullary pyramids (double decussation), making cerebellar deficits ipsilateral
Double decussation of cerebellothalamic and corticospinal pathways keeps unilateral cerebellar signs ipsilateral

questions.sub: Posture and Muscle Tone: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation, Stretch Reflex, and Decerebrate Rigidity
questions.q: What is the 'clasp-knife phenomenon' seen in spasticity (upper motor neuron lesions) when an examiner rapidly flexes or extends a patient's limb?
options: Spasticity initially resists stretch; Golgi tendon organ Ib inhibition then produces clasp-knife release
Complete absence of any resistance from the start of movement
Involuntary rhythmic twitching of the eyelid during sleep
Permanent shortening of tendons with zero neural involvement
questions.explain: In spasticity, hyperactive stretch reflexes initially resist passive movement, until rising tension stimulates Ib Golgi tendon organ afferents to inhibit the alpha motor neurons ('clasp-knife' release). Key detail: Initial strong resistance from hyperactive muscle-spindle stretch reflexes suddenly gives way ('collapses') as high muscle tension activates Golgi tendon organ (Ib) inhibitory interneurons onto homonymous alpha motor neurons (autogenic inhibition).

open.q: Explain the physiological mechanism behind the 'clasp-knife phenomenon' during passive stretch of a spastic limb.
accept: Initial resistance from hyperactive stretch reflexes is abruptly overcome when rising muscle tension activates Golgi tendon organ (Ib) afferents, which inhibit homonymous alpha motor neurons via inhibitory interneurons
High tension activates Golgi tendon organ (Ib) inhibitory interneurons to relax hyperactive extensor/agonist motor neurons after initial stretch resistance

questions.sub: Posture and Muscle Tone: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation, Stretch Reflex, and Decerebrate Rigidity
questions.q: How does 'spasticity' (velocity-dependent clasp-knife hypertonia of upper motor neuron lesions) differ from 'rigidity' (lead-pipe or cogwheel resistance throughout passive motion of basal ganglia disorders)?
options: Spasticity is velocity-dependent with hyperreflexia; rigidity is uniform in flexors and extensors
Spasticity occurs only in peripheral nerve injury while rigidity occurs only in myasthenia gravis
Rigidity causes absent tendon reflexes and muscle fasciculations
Spasticity and rigidity are identical in both mechanism and clinical exam
questions.explain: Spasticity reflects hyperexcitable spinal stretch reflexes from UMN loss (velocity-dependent, clasp-knife, hyperreflexia), whereas rigidity reflects altered supraspinal/basal ganglia tone across flexors and extensors independent of stretch velocity. Key detail: Spasticity is velocity-dependent (increases with faster passive stretch, affects antigravity extensors in legs / flexors in arms, shows clasp-knife release, and pairs with hyperreflexia/Babinski); Rigidity causes uniform resistance across BOTH flexors and extensors throughout slow or fast passive movement without clasp-knife release or hyperreflexia.

open.q: Contrast spasticity (UMN lesion) and rigidity (basal ganglia disorder) in terms of velocity dependence and muscle-group distribution.
accept: Spasticity is velocity-dependent, favors antigravity muscles, shows clasp-knife release, and accompanies hyperreflexia; rigidity produces steady resistance in both flexors and extensors across speeds without clasp-knife release or hyperreflexia
Spasticity: velocity-dependent with clasp-knife release and hyperreflexia; Rigidity: uniform resistance in flexors and extensors across speeds

questions.sub: Posture and Muscle Tone: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation, Stretch Reflex, and Decerebrate Rigidity
questions.q: What is the 'Jendrassik maneuver' (clasping hands and pulling apart while testing a patellar or Achilles tendon reflex), and how does it enhance a sluggish deep tendon reflex?
options: Remote voluntary contraction increases spindle sensitivity and spinal excitability, reinforcing the stretch reflex
It blocks all sensory impulses from entering the dorsal horn
It paralyzes the quadriceps muscle temporarily
It directly stimulates the optic nerve
questions.explain: Reinforcement maneuvers such as the Jendrassik maneuver heighten fusimotor/spinal excitability and help distinguish true hyporeflexia from voluntary guarding or borderline low reflexes. Key detail: Voluntary remote isometric effort (like pulling clasped hands) increases descending facilitation and/or gamma motor neuron bias onto muscle spindles, increasing spindle afferent sensitivity and lowering the threshold for the stretch reflex.

open.q: How does the Jendrassik maneuver reinforce a deep tendon reflex during clinical testing?
accept: Remote voluntary muscle contraction increases gamma/spinal motor excitability and muscle spindle sensitivity, enhancing the stretch reflex response
Increases fusimotor/spinal excitability and spindle sensitivity to reveal/augment the stretch reflex

questions.sub: Locomotion and Spinal Circuits: Central Pattern Generators, Reciprocal Innervation, and Gait
questions.q: How does the 'crossed-extensor reflex' coordinate the opposite limb when one foot steps on a sharp tack and triggers a flexor withdrawal reflex?
options: Ipsilateral flexors withdraw the painful limb; crossed interneurons excite contralateral extensors to support weight
It flexes both legs simultaneously so the person falls backward
It inhibits the contralateral extensor muscles to collapse the supporting leg
It requires conscious input from the primary auditory cortex
questions.explain: The crossed-extensor reflex provides automatic postural support on the contralateral limb while the ipsilateral limb withdraws from a painful stimulus. Key detail: While ipsilateral flexor motor neurons are excited and ipsilateral extensors are inhibited to lift the injured foot away from the tack, crossing spinal interneurons EXCITATE contralateral extensor motor neurons and INHIBIT contralateral flexors to stiffen the opposite leg and support body weight during withdrawal.

open.q: Explain how the crossed-extensor reflex supports posture on the opposite limb during an ipsilateral flexor withdrawal reflex.
accept: Crossing interneurons excite contralateral extensor motor neurons and inhibit contralateral flexors so the opposite limb extends/stiffens to bear body weight while the ipsilateral limb withdraws
Excites contralateral extensors and inhibits contralateral flexors to support body weight while the painful limb withdraws

questions.sub: Cerebellum: Functional Divisions, Circuitry, and Motor Learning
questions.q: What is 'rebound phenomenon (Stewart-Holmes sign)' in a patient with a cerebellar lesion?
options: Sudden release of resistance causes limb overshoot because cerebellar antagonist braking is impaired
The arm immediately drops limp to the floor without any movement
The pupil constricts brightly when the arm is released
The patient feels sharp pain in the opposite big toe
questions.explain: Lack of timely cerebellar braking and antagonist activation causes the limb to overshoot ('rebound') when resistance is suddenly removed. Key detail: When the patient pulls forcefully against the examiner's resistance (e.g., elbow flexion) and the examiner abruptly lets go, the limb overshoots excessively because cerebellar braking/antagonist timing is impaired.

open.q: Describe the rebound phenomenon (Stewart-Holmes sign) and state what it indicates about cerebellar function.
accept: Excessive limb overshoot when resistance to an active contraction is suddenly released, reflecting impaired cerebellar braking and agonist-antagonist timing
Excessive overshoot of a contracted limb after sudden release of resistance due to impaired cerebellar braking

questions.sub: Basal Ganglia: Direct, Indirect, and Nigrostriatal Pathways
questions.q: Which cortical neurotransmitter is used by the 'corticostriate projection' from the cerebral cortex onto medium spiny neurons of the striatum?
options: Glutamate (excitatory)
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
Glycine
questions.explain: Widespread regions of the cerebral cortex send excitatory glutamatergic projections into the striatum, where dopamine from the SNc modulates how corticostriate inputs drive D1 (direct) versus D2 (indirect) pathways.

open.q: Which excitatory neurotransmitter do cortical pyramidal neurons release onto striatal medium spiny neurons in the corticostriate pathway?
accept: Glutamate
Glutamate (excitatory)

questions.sub: Posture and Muscle Tone: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation, Stretch Reflex, and Decerebrate Rigidity
questions.q: What are 'tonic neck reflexes' and 'tonic labyrinthine reflexes' in posture control, and when are they prominently unmasked in humans?
options: Tonic neck reflexes respond to head-on-body position; tonic labyrinthine reflexes respond to head orientation relative to gravity
Tonic neck reflexes respond to sound; tonic labyrinthine reflexes respond to visual acuity
Both reflexes are voluntary cortical movements used only in adults
Tonic labyrinthine reflexes are mediated by taste and olfactory receptors
questions.explain: Tonic neck and tonic labyrinthine reflexes adjust antigravity posture based on head-on-body angle and head-in-gravity orientation, becoming overt when descending cortical/cerebellar inhibition is lost.

open.q: Contrast the sensory origins of tonic neck reflexes and tonic labyrinthine reflexes and state when they become clinically prominent.
accept: Tonic neck reflexes originate from cervical neck proprioceptors/receptors responding to head position relative to the body; tonic labyrinthine reflexes originate from vestibular otolith organs responding to head tilt relative to gravity; both become prominent when higher inhibitory control is lost (e.g., severe brain injury/decerebration)
Tonic neck: cervical receptors (head relative to body); Tonic labyrinthine: otolith organs (head relative to gravity); unmasked by severe brain injury

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 72-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is treated with high-dose levodopa/carbidopa. His bradykinesia and rigidity improve markedly, but he begins exhibiting writhing, purposeless, dance-like movements of his face, neck, and limbs ('peak-dose dyskinesia / chorea'). How does excess dopaminergic stimulation in the striatum produce dyskinesia?
options: Excess striatal dopamine over-facilitates the direct pathway and suppresses the indirect pathway, disinhibiting thalamus
Excess dopamine destroys all alpha motor neurons in the lumbar cord
Levodopa blocks acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Excess dopamine causes cerebellar flocculonodular infarction
questions.explain: Dopaminergic excess tips the basal ganglia balance too far toward thalamocortical disinhibition (hyperkinesia/dyskinesia), requiring careful levodopa dose adjustment or amantadine. Key detail: Excess dopamine over-excites D1 direct-pathway neurons and over-inhibits D2 indirect-pathway neurons, excessively reducing tonic GABAergic inhibition from GPi/SNr onto the motor thalamus and causing excessive thalamocortical disinhibition.

open.q: Explain the basal ganglia circuit mechanism behind levodopa-induced dyskinesia (chorea) in a patient with Parkinson's disease.
accept: Excess dopamine over-activates the D1 direct pathway and suppresses the D2 indirect pathway, lowering GPi/SNr inhibitory output onto the motor thalamus and causing excessive thalamocortical excitation
Excessive D1 facilitation and D2 inhibition reduce GPi/SNr brake on the motor thalamus, causing thalamocortical overactivity

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 46-year-old woman with advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) shows BOTH upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) AND lower motor neuron signs (muscle weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, hyporeflexia) in her limbs with spared extraocular muscles and preserved sensation. Which two motor neuron populations degenerate in ALS?
options: Upper motor neurons in the motor cortex/corticospinal tracts AND lower motor neurons in the brainstem motor nuclei and spinal cord anterior horns
Retinal ganglion cells and cochlear hair cells
Olfactory sensory neurons and taste receptor cells
Cerebellar granule cells and striatal cholinergic interneurons
questions.explain: ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disease affecting both upper motor neurons (cortex/corticospinal tract) and lower motor neurons (anterior horn/bulbar motor nuclei) while typically sparing sensory pathways, cognition early on, and ocular motor nuclei.

open.q: Which two motor neuron populations degenerate in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) to produce mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs?
accept: Upper motor neurons (motor cortex and corticospinal tracts) and lower motor neurons (spinal cord anterior horn cells and brainstem motor nuclei)
Upper motor neurons and lower motor neurons

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 54-year-old man has a middle-aged woman's walk characterized by his pelvis dipping downward on the RIGHT side each time he lifts his RIGHT foot off the ground during the swing phase ('Trendelenburg sign / Trendelenburg gait'). Which muscle group on the LEFT (stance) side is weak, and which nerve innervates it?
options: Left hip abductors (gluteus medius and gluteus minimus), innervated by the left superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1)
Right quadriceps femoris, innervated by the femoral nerve
Left gastrocnemius, innervated by the tibial nerve
Right iliopsoas, innervated by the obturator nerve
questions.explain: During single-leg stance on the left foot, the left gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve) contract to stabilize the pelvis and prevent the unsupported right side of the pelvis from dropping; left gluteal weakness causes a positive Trendelenburg sign (pelvic drop on the right swing side).

open.q: When a patient's pelvis drops on the right side during right-leg swing (positive Trendelenburg sign), which side's hip abductors are weak and which nerve innervates them?
accept: Left hip abductors (gluteus medius and gluteus minimus), innervated by the left superior gluteal nerve
Left gluteus medius and minimus; left superior gluteal nerve

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 29-year-old man undergoes neurosurgical resection of a vascular lesion in the right middle cerebral artery territory that damages the right supplementary motor area (SMA) and right premotor cortex while sparing the primary motor cortex (area 4). He has no fixed paralysis, yet struggles to perform smooth bimanual tasks (such as holding a jar with one hand and unscrewing the lid with the other) and shows difficulty initiating self-paced sequential finger movements. Which deficit is highlighted?
options: Impaired motor planning, sequencing, and bimanual coordination from SMA/premotor damage despite preserved primary motor cortex (area 4) execution
Complete deafness in the left ear
Loss of pupillary constriction to light
Inability to taste sweet foods
questions.explain: Area 6 (SMA and premotor cortex) programs and coordinates sequential and bimanual movements before passing commands to primary motor cortex (area 4) and descending motor tracts.

open.q: What motor deficit is characteristic of damage to the supplementary motor area (SMA) and premotor cortex when primary motor cortex (area 4) is spared?
accept: Impaired motor planning, sequential movement programming, and bimanual coordination despite preserved primary motor execution
Deficits in motor planning, sequencing, and bimanual coordination with preserved primary motor cortex output

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 61-year-old man with neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis) or severe vitamin B12 deficiency loses large-fiber proprioceptive/Ia/II sensory input from his lower limbs. When standing with feet together, he remains steady with eyes OPEN but sways or falls immediately when closing his eyes ('positive Romberg test'). Why does closing his eyes cause loss of balance?
options: Vision compensates for proprioceptive loss; closing the eyes removes that input and unmasks sensory ataxia
Closing the eyes paralyzes the stapedius muscle
Romberg sign is positive only in patients with normal proprioception and blindness
Closing the eyes destroys the basal ganglia immediately
questions.explain: A positive Romberg test (markedly worse sway/falling with eyes closed vs eyes open) indicates sensory/proprioceptive ataxia (dorsal columns/peripheral proprioceptive afferents), whereas cerebellar ataxia causes unsteadiness even with eyes OPEN. Key detail: When proprioceptive somatosensory feedback from the legs is impaired, vision and vestibular input compensate while eyes are open; closing the eyes removes visual compensation, exposing the underlying proprioceptive/sensory ataxia.

open.q: Explain why a patient with lower-limb proprioceptive loss sways or falls when closing their eyes during the Romberg test.
accept: Closing the eyes eliminates visual cues that were compensating for impaired proprioceptive feedback from the legs, unmasking sensory ataxia
Removes visual compensation for lost proprioceptive input from the lower limbs, revealing sensory ataxia

questions.sub: Posture and Muscle Tone: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation, Stretch Reflex, and Decerebrate Rigidity
questions.q: Which sensory afferent fibers mediate the rapid 'monosynaptic stretch (myotatic) reflex' (such as the patellar tendon jerk), and where do they synapse?
options: Group Ia muscle-spindle afferents monosynaptically excite homonymous alpha motor neurons
Group Ib Golgi tendon organ afferents — synapse directly onto homonymous extensor motor neurons to cause excitation
C-fiber nociceptors — synapse directly onto alpha motor neurons
Olfactory receptor axons — synapse directly onto lumbar motor neurons
questions.explain: The stretch reflex is the classic vertebrate monosynaptic reflex: stretch of muscle spindle -> Group Ia afferent -> direct excitatory synapse onto homonymous alpha motor neuron -> muscle contraction. Key detail: Group Ia muscle spindle primary afferents — synapse DIRECTLY (monosynaptically) onto homonymous alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord ventral horn (while also exciting Ia inhibitory interneurons to antagonist muscles).

open.q: Name the sensory afferent fiber responsible for the monosynaptic stretch reflex and identify its direct spinal cord target.
accept: Group Ia afferent fibers (from muscle spindles); synapse directly onto homonymous alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord ventral horn
Group Ia muscle spindle afferents; homonymous alpha motor neurons

questions.sub: Posture and Muscle Tone: Alpha-Gamma Coactivation, Stretch Reflex, and Decerebrate Rigidity
questions.q: Contrast the sensory receptor, afferent fiber type, and reflex effect of the 'muscle spindle' versus the 'Golgi tendon organ (GTO)':
options: Muscle spindle: parallel, senses length via Ia/II afferents; Golgi tendon organ: in series, senses tension via Ib afferents
Muscle spindle: in series, senses tension via Ib afferents; Golgi tendon organ: parallel, senses length via Ia afferents
Both receptors lie in tendons and detect only muscle tension
Both receptors lie in muscle bellies and inhibit the homonymous motor neuron
questions.explain: Muscle spindles sit in parallel to sense length/stretch (Ia/II), whereas Golgi tendon organs sit in series in tendons to sense force/tension (Ib) and inhibit homonymous motor neurons when tension becomes excessive.

open.q: Contrast the anatomical arrangement (in parallel vs in series), stimulus detected, afferent fiber class, and reflex effect of muscle spindles versus Golgi tendon organs.
accept: Muscle spindles lie in parallel with muscle fibers, sense length/stretch via Ia/II afferents, and excite homonymous alpha motor neurons; Golgi tendon organs lie in series in tendons, sense tension via Ib afferents, and inhibit homonymous alpha motor neurons via Ib interneurons
Spindles: in parallel, length/stretch (Ia/II), excite homonymous motor neurons; GTOs: in series, tension (Ib), inhibit homonymous motor neurons

questions.sub: Cerebellum: Functional Divisions, Circuitry, and Motor Learning
questions.q: What is 'decomposed movement (asynergia)' in cerebellar disease, and why do multi-joint movements look jerky and broken into sequential single-joint steps?
options: Cerebellar dysfunction breaks smooth multi-joint actions into jerky, sequential single-joint movements
Because the skeletal muscles lose all myosin filaments
Because the patient is intentionally moving slowly to avoid dizziness
Because the vestibular semicircular canals fuse together
questions.explain: Smooth reaching requires predictive feedforward coordination of interaction torques across multiple joints; cerebellar lesions break multi-joint movements into jerky, decomposed components. Key detail: Because the cerebellum coordinates simultaneous multi-joint torques and reciprocal agonist/antagonist timing across shoulder, elbow, and wrist; without cerebellar coordination, the patient performs each joint angle one step at a time instead of smoothly blending them.

open.q: Explain what 'decomposed movement' is in cerebellar dysfunction and why it occurs.
accept: Breaking a smooth multi-joint movement into separate, jerky single-joint steps due to loss of cerebellar feedforward coordination of multi-joint torques and agonist-antagonist timing
Performing multi-joint movements as separate jerky single-joint steps due to loss of cerebellar multi-joint coordination

questions.sub: Locomotion and Spinal Circuits: Central Pattern Generators, Reciprocal Innervation, and Gait
questions.q: Which 'descending brainstem motor tract' originates in the magnocellular 'red nucleus' of the midbrain, crosses in the ventral tegmental decussation, and facilitates contralateral limb FLEXOR motor neurons (especially in the upper limbs)?
options: Rubrospinal tract
Lateral vestibulospinal tract
Anterior corticospinal tract
Olfactory tract
questions.explain: The rubrospinal tract travels in the lateral funiculus alongside the lateral corticospinal tract and facilitates flexor motor neurons while inhibiting extensors in the contralateral limbs.

open.q: Which descending tract arises from the midbrain red nucleus and facilitates contralateral limb flexor motor neurons?
accept: Rubrospinal tract
Rubrospinal

questions.sub: Locomotion and Spinal Circuits: Central Pattern Generators, Reciprocal Innervation, and Gait
questions.q: During normal human walking, how does 'sensory load/stretch feedback' from ankle extensors and hip flexors interact with spinal locomotor circuits to time the transition from 'stance' to 'swing'?
options: Stance-limb unloading and hip extension permit swing initiation, preventing premature lift-off
The leg lifts off the ground regardless of whether full body weight is resting on it
Sensory feedback from the foot blocks stepping completely during walking
Transition from stance to swing is controlled solely by the optic nerve
questions.explain: Load receptors (Golgi tendon organs) and hip position sensors prevent premature swing initiation while a limb is still loaded, ensuring safe weight transfer onto the opposite leg. Key detail: Unloading of weight/force on the stance limb (reduced Ib/load signals) together with hip extension/stretch signals triggers the swing-phase transition so the leg does not lift off while still bearing full body weight.

open.q: How do limb unloading and hip position signals help regulate the transition from the stance phase to the swing phase during walking?
accept: Unloading of limb weight/force and hip extension signals permit/trigger the transition into swing phase, preventing premature leg lift while bearing weight
Unloading of stance-limb weight and hip extension trigger swing initiation so a loaded limb is not lifted prematurely

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 59-year-old man has a small ischemic stroke restricted to the 'left internal capsule (posterior limb)'. He develops contralateral right-sided spastic hemiparesis, hyperreflexia, and a right Babinski sign, with minimal or no impairment of eye movements or facial sensation. Why does a posterior limb internal capsule lesion produce such dense contralateral motor deficits?
options: Corticospinal fibres are densely packed in the posterior limb, so a small lesion causes dense contralateral UMN weakness
The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains only lower motor neuron cell bodies
The internal capsule carries only visual fibers from the retina
A left internal capsule stroke causes ipsilateral lower motor neuron flaccid paralysis
questions.explain: Because corticospinal axons are densely packed in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, even a small lacunar infarct produces prominent contralateral upper motor neuron hemiparesis/hemiplegia. Key detail: Corticospinal tract fibers converge tightly within the posterior limb of the internal capsule, so a small focal lacunar stroke here interrupts a high density of descending upper motor neuron axons destined for contralateral spinal motor neurons.

open.q: Explain why a small focal stroke in the posterior limb of the internal capsule causes prominent contralateral upper motor neuron weakness.
accept: Descending corticospinal tract fibers are tightly packed together in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, so a small lesion interrupts a large proportion of upper motor neuron output to the contralateral limbs
Corticospinal fibers are densely bundled in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, making small lesions cause dense contralateral UMN deficits

questions.sub: Corticospinal tract
questions.q: A small infarct selectively damages corticospinal fibres at the pyramidal decussation. Which deficit is most likely below the lesion?
options: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature
Contralateral loss of fine voluntary movement below the lesion
Bilateral loss of vestibular reflexes
Isolated flaccid paralysis of facial muscles
questions.explain: Most corticospinal fibres cross in the caudal medulla at the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract. A lesion at or above this crossing produces contralateral weakness below the lesion; a lesion in the spinal cord below the decussation produces ipsilateral upper motor neuron signs.

open.q: Where do most corticospinal fibres decussate, and what is the side of weakness caused by a lesion above this crossing?
accept: At the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla; contralateral weakness
Caudal medulla; contralateral motor deficit

questions.sub: Corticospinal tract
questions.q: A patient has weakness of skilled finger movements after a lesion involving the lateral corticospinal tract. Which anatomical feature best explains this deficit?
options: Its fibres terminate exclusively in autonomic nuclei
It provides important control of distal limb muscles through spinal interneurons and motor neurons
It carries proprioceptive information from muscle spindles
It is the principal descending pathway for vestibulo-ocular reflexes
questions.explain: The lateral corticospinal tract is especially important for fractionated voluntary movement of distal limb muscles, including the hand. Many fibres influence motor neuron pools through spinal interneurons, with some direct corticomotoneuronal connections particularly relevant to hand control.

open.q: What is the principal motor role of the lateral corticospinal tract?
accept: Fine, fractionated voluntary control of distal limb muscles, especially the hand
Skilled voluntary movement of distal limbs

questions.sub: Upper motor neuron signs
questions.q: A patient develops an extensor plantar response after a stroke affecting descending motor pathways. Which mechanism best accounts for this finding in an adult?
options: Loss of descending corticospinal inhibition unmasks a normally suppressed plantar response
Increased activity of lower motor neurons in the anterior horn destroys the plantar reflex
Damage to dorsal columns causes involuntary toe extension
Excessive activity of the spinothalamic tract activates toe extensors
questions.explain: An extensor plantar response (Babinski sign) in an adult is a pathological sign of corticospinal or other upper motor neuron pathway dysfunction. It reflects loss of normal descending control over the plantar response; it is not simply a sign of increased lower motor neuron activity.

open.q: What does an extensor plantar (Babinski) response indicate in an adult?
accept: Upper motor neuron/corticospinal pathway dysfunction
Corticospinal tract lesion
Loss of descending control of the plantar response

questions.sub: Brainstem descending pathways
questions.q: A patient with a brainstem lesion has impaired postural extension and reduced antigravity extensor activity. Which descending pathway normally contributes strongly to this function?
options: Vestibulospinal tract
Spinothalamic tract
Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway
Medial longitudinal fasciculus
questions.explain: Vestibulospinal pathways arise from vestibular nuclei and facilitate extensor (antigravity) muscle activity, helping maintain balance and postural stability. The lateral vestibulospinal tract has a particularly important influence on extensor tone.

open.q: Which brainstem descending pathway facilitates antigravity extensor activity and supports posture?
accept: Vestibulospinal tract
Lateral vestibulospinal tract

questions.sub: Brainstem descending pathways
questions.q: A lesion interrupts descending fibres from the pontomedullary reticular formation. Which function is most likely to be disturbed?
options: Automatic regulation of posture, muscle tone and locomotor-related activity
Conscious discrimination of two-point touch
Transmission of visual information to the occipital cortex
Voluntary control of the extraocular muscles only
questions.explain: Reticulospinal pathways arise from the brainstem reticular formation and contribute to postural adjustments, regulation of muscle tone, locomotor activity and coordination of automatic movements. They interact with vestibulospinal and corticospinal systems.

open.q: State two functions of the reticulospinal pathways.
accept: Regulation of posture and muscle tone; contribution to locomotor and automatic movements
Postural control and regulation of muscle tone

questions.sub: Cerebellar function
questions.q: A patient has truncal instability, a broad-based gait and difficulty maintaining equilibrium, but relatively preserved limb strength. Which cerebellar region is most likely affected?
options: Flocculonodular lobe
Lateral cerebellar hemisphere
Dentate nucleus alone
Anterior horn of the spinal cord
questions.explain: The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) is closely connected with vestibular nuclei and is important for balance, equilibrium and coordination of eye movements. Lesions can produce truncal ataxia and gait instability.

open.q: Which cerebellar lobe is most closely associated with equilibrium and vestibular function?
accept: Flocculonodular lobe
Vestibulocerebellum

questions.sub: Cerebellar lesions
questions.q: A patient with a unilateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion overshoots the target during finger-to-nose testing on the same side. Which principle explains the side of the limb deficit?
options: Cerebellar influence on limb movement is functionally ipsilateral
Cerebellar output controls only the contralateral lower limb
The cerebellum has no influence on voluntary movement
All cerebellar fibres cross once and therefore produce contralateral signs
questions.explain: Cerebellar lesions typically cause ipsilateral limb ataxia. Cerebellar output crosses to influence contralateral motor systems, while corticospinal output crosses again before reaching the limb, resulting in a net ipsilateral functional relationship.

open.q: Why do cerebellar hemisphere lesions usually produce ipsilateral limb ataxia?
accept: Because cerebellar motor influence undergoes a double-crossing arrangement, giving a net ipsilateral effect
Net effect of cerebellar pathways is ipsilateral

questions.sub: Cerebellar lesions
questions.q: During examination, a patient shows intention tremor, dysmetria and decomposition of movement on the right. Which structure is most likely involved?
options: Right cerebellar hemisphere or its connections
Left primary visual cortex
Right dorsal column in the cervical cord only
Bilateral vestibular nuclei exclusively
questions.explain: Limb dysmetria, intention tremor and decomposition of movement are characteristic of cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction and generally occur ipsilateral to the lesion. The findings reflect impaired coordination and error correction rather than primary loss of muscle power.

open.q: Name three characteristic findings of a cerebellar hemisphere lesion.
accept: Ipsilateral dysmetria, intention tremor and decomposition of movement
Dysmetria, intention tremor, decomposition of movement

questions.sub: Cerebellar function
questions.q: A patient can generate muscle power but has difficulty planning and timing rapid, skilled sequences of voluntary movement. Which cerebellar division is most likely affected?
options: Cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres)
Vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe)
Spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate zone)
Flocculus alone
questions.explain: The cerebrocerebellum, formed mainly by the lateral cerebellar hemispheres, participates in planning, timing and coordination of complex skilled voluntary movements. Vestibulocerebellar lesions primarily disturb balance and eye movements, while spinocerebellar lesions commonly impair posture, gait and ongoing limb coordination.

open.q: Which functional division of the cerebellum is especially involved in planning and timing skilled voluntary movements?
accept: Cerebrocerebellum
Lateral cerebellar hemispheres

questions.sub: Basal ganglia
questions.q: A patient with Parkinson disease has bradykinesia. Reduced activity in which pathway normally contributes to this difficulty initiating movement?
options: Direct striatal pathway facilitating thalamocortical activity
Nigrostriatal dopaminergic projection that modulates striatal output
Spinocerebellar pathway carrying unconscious proprioception
Lateral vestibulospinal tract maintaining extensor tone
questions.explain: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta reduces facilitation of the direct pathway and removes inhibition of the indirect pathway, increasing inhibitory basal ganglia output to the thalamus.

open.q: Which dopaminergic projection degenerates in Parkinson disease?
accept: Nigrostriatal pathway
Substantia nigra pars compacta to striatum
